text: A hands-on trace through both 3-qubit codes end to end, reusing the verified tables from this chapter — the goal is to be able to do this by hand, confidently, before moving to the more abstract stabilizer formalism in Chapter 4.

Trace 1: start from logical one, the all-ones state, and suppose an X error strikes qubit 2. The state becomes 101. Measuring Z1Z2 compares qubits 1 and 2, 1 versus 0, a disagreement, giving outcome 1. Measuring Z2Z3 compares qubits 2 and 3, 0 versus 1, also a disagreement, giving outcome 1. The syndrome is 1,1, and the Lesson 10 table says that syndrome means flip qubit 2 — doing so turns 101 back into 111, fully restored. This matches the table exactly, confirming the syndrome only depends on where the error hit, never on alpha or beta.

Trace 2: start from logical zero in the phase-flip code, written as 000 in plus-minus shorthand, and suppose a Z error strikes qubit 3, giving 001. Measuring X1X2 compares qubits 1 and 2, 0 versus 0, agreement, outcome 0. Measuring X2X3 compares qubits 2 and 3, 0 versus 1, disagreement, outcome 1. The syndrome is 0,1, and the Lesson 11 table says apply Z to qubit 3 — doing so flips it back from minus to plus, restoring 000 fully.

Notice both traces follow the identical six-step shape: state the error, compute each stabilizer's outcome directly from the physical bits touched, assemble the syndrome, look up the unique correction, apply it, verify. That shape generalizes, unchanged, to every stabilizer code in this course — the Steane code's six stabilizers in Chapter 4 and the surface code's many four-qubit stabilizers in Chapter 5 are traced through this exact same procedure, just with more stabilizers and larger syndromes to read.
Next, Chapter 4 introduces the stabilizer formalism — the abstract language that generalizes everything you've just traced by hand.
